name: Checklist
css:
/* ONE SPRING PER ROW, AND EVERYTHING IS READ OFF IT. The
   box filling, the tick drawing, the rule crossing the words
   and the words giving up their ink are four readings of a
   single number, not four things animated toward the same
   moment. Four transitions is four chances for one to arrive
   early and break the illusion that this is one event. */
const t = useSpring(on ? 1 : 0, bounce);

/* WHERE THE OVERSHOOT IS ALLOWED, AND WHERE IT IS NOT. A
   spring goes past its target and comes back, which is what
   makes a check feel like a press — but only some of these
   survive it. The fill takes the raw value and swells past
   full. The tick and the rule take it CLAMPED: a tick that
   overshoots draws itself past its own end and pulls back,
   which is a glitch rather than a bounce. One spring, two
   readings, and the difference is one clamp. */
transform: `scale(${t})`            /* raw    */
strokeDashoffset={1 - clamp(t, 0, 1)} /* clamped */

/* THE TICK IS DRAWN, NOT FADED. pathLength="1" normalises the
   dash to the stroke's own length, so the offset is a
   fraction rather than a number measured off this particular
   path — change the checkmark and nothing else has to know. */
<path d="M6 12.4 L10.3 16.7 L18 7.6" pathLength={1}
      strokeDasharray={1} strokeDashoffset={1 - t} />

/* THE RULE FOLLOWS THE TICK, IT DOES NOT RACE IT. A window on
   the same number rather than a second timer, so there is
   nothing to keep in step. Started together they read as one
   wipe across the row; started apart they read as cause and
   effect. */
const cut = clamp((t - 0.12) / 0.72, 0, 1);

/* AND IT IS SCALED, NOT GROWN. A width in pixels needs the
   word measured; scaleX from the left edge needs nothing, and
   a 1.5px line has no corner for a scale to distort. The span
   is sized to the WORDS rather than the row, so the rule
   stops where the text does. */
transform: `scaleX(${cut})`

/* AND FINISHING THE LIST TAKES THE FLOOR OUT FROM UNDER IT.
   Not a state — every task ticked IS the finish, so unticking
   one during the three seconds makes this false on the same
   render and the rows climb back without anything having to
   remember that they had fallen. */
const fell = done.every(Boolean);

/* Down is a duration with gravity's shape in it — it starts at
   nothing and gains, which is what easeIn is — and the fourth
   keyframe is the rebound, which is the difference between
   landing and being placed. Up is a SPRING, because coming
   back is the list reasserting itself rather than anything
   being dropped, and because a spring interrupts cleanly:
   untick a task halfway through the fall and the row is picked
   up from wherever it had got to. */
animate={fell ? { y: [0, drop, drop - 9, drop], rotate: tilt }
              : { y: 0, rotate: 0 }}
transition={fell ? { duration: 0.62, delay: wait,
                     times: [0, 0.66, 0.84, 1],
                     ease: ["easeIn", "easeOut", "easeIn"] }
                 : { type: "spring", stiffness: 420, damping: 26 }}

/* Every row falls the SAME distance, because the heap keeps
   the spacing the list had — three touching blocks losing
   their support fall together. So the sequence comes from when
   they let go rather than how far they travel: the bottom row
   first, 45ms apart, which is a stack collapsing from
   underneath. */

/* THE FILL OPENS FROM THE MIDDLE, inside a ring that never
   changes. A checkbox that swaps its background is a
   different colour arriving; one whose fill grows out of the
   centre is the box being filled in, which is what the word
   means. */

params.label: Box
params.hint: the checkbox

params.label: Bounce
params.hint: how far the box swells past full

name: Palette
css:
/* THE COLOURS ARE PICKED IN OKLCH, which is the whole
   difference between this and the random-hex generator
   everybody writes first. In HSL, "lightness" is a lie:
   hsl(60 90% 50%) is a bright yellow and hsl(240 90% 50%) is
   a near-black blue — at the same number. A palette built by
   holding L and stepping the hue comes out with one swatch
   that glows and one you can barely see.

   OKLCH is perceptually uniform, so a ramp written in it is a
   ramp you can actually see. Generated there, converted to
   hex on the way out, because hex is what somebody wants to
   paste into their own file. */

/* AND THEY ARE A RAMP, NOT A SPIN. Four random hues do not
   make a palette however even their lightness is. What makes
   a set look chosen is that it agrees about one thing and
   varies another: these hold a hue family and ramp the
   lightness across it, which is what a person does by hand. */
const L = 0.9 - p * 0.5;                        /* light to deep */
const C = 0.05 + Math.sin(p * Math.PI) * 0.105; /* vivid in the middle */
const H = base + i * step;                      /* 16-34 degrees apart */

/* CHROMA PEAKS IN THE MIDDLE rather than being held flat, for
   the same reason a very light and a very dark colour cannot
   be vivid: there is no room left in the gamut, and asking
   for it is what makes generated palettes go chalky at one
   end and muddy at the other. */

/* ONE SET IN THREE GETS AN ACCENT — the last swatch jumps to
   the far side of the wheel. A ramp on its own is tasteful and
   slightly dull, and the odd complement is what stops a run of
   generated sets feeling like one set regenerated. */

/* THE SWAP IS HIDDEN, and that is the whole motion. Each
   swatch draws into a circle and the colour changes at the
   top of that — the frame there is least of it to look at —
   then it spreads back into its slot. You never see a
   crossfade because there is nothing to cross. A palette that
   dissolved from old to new would show you every muddy colour
   in between, and none of those are in either palette. */
const d = swellOf(t);                     /* 0 at rest, 1 drawn in */
const shown = t >= 0.4 ? next[i] : now[i];

/* AND THEY ALL GO AT ONCE. The obvious version staggers them,
   so the change travels along the bar — which looks good and
   says the wrong thing. A wave says these are a sequence and
   that one caused the next. They are a set, and one press
   replaced all of them in the same instant. */

/* THE BLUR RIDES THE MOTION AND IS ZERO AT REST. It has to
   be: an alpha-contrast filter blurs everything under it, so
   a standing blur smears neighbouring colours into one
   gradient. Because every swatch is a single solid colour at
   every frame, the filter can only ever bridge the GAP
   between two of them — which is liquid. Blur applied inside
   a colour is just smear. */
const heat = Math.sin(Math.PI * t) * 5;

params.label: Colours
params.hint: how many in the set

params.label: Morph
params.hint: how quickly a colour changes

name: Aspect ratio
css:
/* THE THREE FORMATS HAVE THE SAME AREA, and that is the
   whole idea. The common build fixes the width and lets the
   height do whatever the ratio says — which makes the
   landscape a third of the portrait, so switching feels like
   the picture GREW rather than like it was cropped.

   Equal area is what a crop actually is: the same amount of
   picture, held a different way. Within 0.02% across all
   three, and every shape fits inside one 276 square, so the
   block's bounding box never changes and the wall cannot
   rescale it mid-move. */
land   276 x 207     /* 4:3 */
square 239 x 239     /* 1:1 */
tall   207 x 276     /* 3:4 */

/* WIDTH AND HEIGHT, NEVER A SCALE. The same rule the detail
   overlay's block follows and for the same reason: a scaled
   box drags its corner radius with it, and the corner has to
   read as the same rounded frame throughout rather than as a
   rectangle being stretched. */
transition: width 520ms cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1),
            height 520ms cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1);

/* COVER is what keeps the picture undistorted while the frame
   moves, so this reads as a crop changing — which is what it
   is — rather than as an image being squashed. Contain would
   letterbox it and fill would stretch it. The source is 3:4
   and is not cropped in the file, so one picture makes all
   three and the portrait tab is the whole illustration. */
background-size: cover;
background-position: center;

/* THE STAGE IS THE FULL SQUARE and never changes size, so the
   picture is centred in a box that is not moving. Sizing the
   stage to the picture instead makes the tabs below it climb
   and drop as the shape changes — the one thing here with no
   business moving. */

/* ONE THUMB SLIDING, not three backgrounds fading. A fill
   that appears under the new tab while another disappears is
   two events; a thumb that travels is one, and it is the one
   that says these three are positions of the same control.

   And it LEADS: its duration is a fraction of the picture's
   rather than a number of its own. A control that takes as
   long as the thing it controls feels like it did not hear
   you; one that arrives first reads as the cause of what
   follows. */
transition: transform calc(var(--asp-ms) * 0.55) ...;

/* THE ICONS ARE THE SHAPES. Drawn rather than imported —
   lucide does ship a rectangle in each orientation, but here
   the icon is not a symbol FOR the format, it IS the format,
   so it has to be at the real ratio. Same constant area as
   the pictures, or three marks of visibly different size
   would say the formats are different sizes. */

params.label: Morph
params.hint: how quickly it changes shape

params.label: Corner
params.hint: the picture's radius

name: Tilt card
css:
/* IT SINKS, IT DOES NOT LIFT. Every tilt card on the
   internet rotates TOWARD the cursor: the corner nearest you
   rises to meet you and the card reads as a slab of glass
   catching the light. This one does the opposite — the point
   you are over goes AWAY and the far side comes up.

   One minus sign, and it is the whole component. A surface
   that rises to your finger is being displayed to you; a
   surface that gives under it is being touched. */
const rx = -ny * tilt;   /* cursor at the top → top goes back */
const ry =  nx * tilt;   /* cursor right → right goes back  */

/* THE ROTATION ALONE IS NOT ENOUGH. A rotation about the
   centre is symmetric — near side down, far side up by the
   same amount — and on its own it reads as a card pivoting,
   not as one being pressed. What makes it a press is that the
   darkest point tracks the pointer: a depression catches
   shadow at its deepest, and the rim opposite catches light.
   These two gradients do at least as much work as the
   transform, and neither convinces on its own. */
background-image:
  radial-gradient(42% 34% at X% Y%, rgba(9,14,28,0.25), transparent),
  radial-gradient(52% 42% at (100-X)% (100-Y)%, rgba(255,255,255,0.15), transparent);

/* THE SHADOW TIGHTENS. A thing pressed into a surface has
   less air under it, so the gap closes and the shadow draws
   in. Growing it on hover is the reflex — it is what a card
   that LIFTS would do — and it fights every other cue here. */
box-shadow: 0 mix(20, 9, lit)px mix(44, 24, lit)px -8px rgba(15,23,42,0.2);

/* ONE PAIR OF NUMBERS IS THE STATE. Two springs hold where
   the pointer is, normalised to -1..1, and the rotation, both
   gradients and the shadow are all read off them — three
   readings of one number rather than three things animating
   towards the same place. The spring is on the POSITION, not
   on the rotation, so they cannot disagree about where the
   finger is.

   Sprung rather than tracked one-to-one because a card with
   no weight follows the cursor exactly and reads as a texture
   pinned to the mouse. The lag is what gives it mass. */
const sx = useSpring(on ? nx : 0);
const sy = useSpring(on ? ny : 0);

/* PERSPECTIVE ON THE FRAME, not on the card. On the card
   itself it is applied per element, so the vanishing point
   rides along with the rotation instead of staying put in the
   room — and the frame is also what the pointer is measured
   against, because asking a rotating object where it is gets
   you an answer that has already turned away. */
perspective: 800px;

params.label: Tilt
params.hint: how far it turns under you

params.label: Shade
params.hint: how deep the dent reads

params.label: Corner
params.hint: the card's radius

name: Now playing
css:
/* ONE NUMBER IS THE STATE, and everything else is read off
   it. A single tween runs 0 → 1 and every position, size,
   radius and type size is a mix() of its two ends — so there
   is no transition anywhere in the stylesheet for the shape.

   With eight CSS transitions there are eight chances for one
   to arrive early and break the illusion that this is one
   object. With one number there are none. */
const p = useTween(open ? 1 : 0, ms);
const mix = (a, b, t) => a + (b - a) * t;

/* EASED, NOT SPRUNG, and the corner is the reason. A spring
   past its target takes every value derived from it along:
   measured, the height reached 492 against a target of 404
   and the radius went with it, dipping under its own end
   value and coming back. That is a wobble, not a bounce.

   Quart-out is cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1) in all but
   name — quick off the mark, lands without ever passing the
   number it is going to. */
const e = 1 - (1 - t) ** 4;

/* SO THE BOUNCE IS A SECOND NUMBER, and it only scales. The
   progress stays monotonic and the composition stays
   internally consistent every frame — the sleeve, the box and the margin
   between them always in the ratio that keeps the corners
   concentric. What bounces is the whole object, uniformly: a
   scale takes the box, the sleeve, the corners and the type
   together, so nothing can get out of step with anything
   else. It is the same picture, briefly smaller.

   Its own LINEAR clock, because the progress above is
   quart-out and near its end for most of the move — a swell
   read off it spikes in the first two frames and is flat for
   the rest. Peak pushed
   late so the object gathers and releases as it lands.

   ON THE CLOSE ONLY. Opening already has its event: the box
   goes 78 → 189 and that is the thing you are meant to watch,
   so a scale on top is a second size change in the same
   direction at the same time. Closing collapses into a bar
   and most of it stops existing — there the dip is something
   to go with the disappearance. */
const u = useTween(open ? 1 : 0, ms, (t) => t);
const swell = Math.sin(Math.PI * clamp(u, 0, 1) ** 1.5);
scale: open ? 1 : 1 - 0.035 * swell;

/* THE COVER IS THE HINGE. It is the only thing on the bar big
   enough to be recognised, so it is what the eye tracks — and
   it never crossfades or disappears. It travels from a 40px
   square to a 64px one without ever leaving the corner it
   started in, and everything else takes its lead from where
   it went.

   ONE MARGIN, BOTH STATES — not one per state. At 10 on the
   bar and 16 on the card the sleeve, the track and the
   transport all slid inward as it opened: a fourth motion
   nobody asked for, on top of the three that are the point.
   The object grows; its frame does not move. */
<span style={{
  left:   10,
  top:    10,
  width:  mix(40, 64, p),
  height: mix(40, 64, p),
}} />

/* THE WIDTH NEVER CHANGES. A bar that also got wider would be
   growing in two directions at once, and the second adds
   nothing: what a player does when it opens is show you more,
   downward. Holding it still also means the transport only
   has to travel rather than resize and travel. */
height: mix(78, 189, p);

/* THE CORNERS ARE CONCENTRIC — the box's radius is the
   sleeve's plus the margin between them. Not a preference:
   two curves offset by a constant distance stay parallel,
   and any other pair pinches at 45°. 32 was picked by eye
   and it was six too many — the card's curve swept wider
   than the artwork's and left its top-left sitting inside a
   bend that had already turned.

   IT IS ALSO WHY THE CORNER CAN BE A KNOB. It was a control
   once and it was removed, because what it set was the box's
   corner on its own: turn it down and the card squared off
   around a sleeve that had not; turn it up and the card's
   curve swept wide of the picture. Every setting but one was
   wrong. What the slider moves now is the SLEEVE, and the box
   is derived — so the pair stays concentric at every value
   and there is no setting that pinches. A knob on a
   relationship, not on one of its halves.

   AND THE OFFSET FADES IN. Ten pixels at every setting,
   including zero, drew a perfectly sharp picture inside a
   card that was still visibly rounded — concentric on paper,
   two different decisions to look at. At radius zero there is
   no curve to stay parallel to, so the rule was answering a
   question nobody had asked there. Scaled by how far up the
   slider you are, it reaches its full ten by the default:
   below that the corners converge until they are square
   together, above it the rule takes over, which is where it
   earns its keep. */
const PAD = 10, CORNER = 16;
const artR = [corner * 40 / 64, corner];        /* 0 → 32 */
const off  = PAD * Math.min(1, corner / CORNER);
border-radius: mix(artR[0] + off, artR[1] + off, p);

/* The parts that only exist in the card are held back to the
   last 40% of the move, so they arrive into a shape that has
   stopped growing rather than sliding about inside one that
   has not. */
const late = clamp((p - 0.6) / 0.4, 0, 1);

/* THE PLAY MARK IS DRAWN, NOT SWAPPED. Two icons exchanged
   is a cut however short you make the crossfade, and this is
   the one control you press more than once — a cut you see
   forty times is the thing you end up looking at.

   So both marks are the SAME two quadrilaterals and the
   difference between them is where eight points are. The
   pause is a pair of bars; the play is that pair with the
   inner edges pulled to the middle and collapsed to a point,
   which is a triangle split down its own axis. Wound the
   same way in both, or the halves turn inside out crossing. */
const PAUSE_L = [6,4, 10,4, 10,20, 6,20];
const PLAY_L  = [6.5,4, 13.25,8, 13.25,16, 6.5,20];

/* THE GOO IS ZERO AT BOTH ENDS. Everything soft here rides
   sin(pi * t), so it is a bulge on the way rather than a
   difference between the two states — press twice and it
   lands on exactly what it started as. The mark squashes
   across as it stretches up, the halves lean in until they
   touch, and the whole thing tips a few degrees and comes
   back level. Changing size without changing volume is what
   reads as soft rather than as redrawn. */
const goo = Math.sin(clamp(t, 0, 1) * Math.PI);
transform: rotate(9deg * goo * dir)
           scale(1 - 0.13 * goo, 1 + 0.11 * goo);

params.label: Corner
params.hint: the sleeve, and the box around it

params.label: Morph
params.hint: how quickly it opens

name: Search
css:
/* ONE OBJECT, NOT TWO. Everything follows from that.

   The obvious build is an icon that fades out and an input
   that fades in — obvious because it is easy, and wrong
   because two things swapping is never mistaken for one thing
   changing, however well the crossfade is tuned. So there is
   a single box whose WIDTH is the state, with the icon and
   the field both inside it the whole time.

   Which turns the interesting problems into geometry rather
   than choreography. */

/* 1 · THE LENS NEVER MOVES relative to the box. It sits at a
      fixed inset from the left edge — and at the closed width
      that inset happens to centre it:

        (44 - 18) / 2 = 13

      13 is also the padding the open field wants. One number
      is both "centred in a circle" and "aligned in a field",
      so the lens travelling leftward across the page is not
      an animation anybody wrote. It is the box growing around
      a mark that stayed put. */
left: var(--inset);

/* 2 · IT GROWS FROM ITS MIDDLE, so the composition stays
      centred at every frame. From the left would pin the lens
      and throw the field off centre; from the right would
      slide the lens across the page. Neither is the object
      transforming, and both are what you get by accident. */

/* 3 · ONE SHAPE RULE. Fully round at every width: at 44 it is
      a circle, at 320 a pill, and those are the same
      statement rather than two ends of a tween. The radius
      used to interpolate 22 → 13, which was a second thing
      that had to agree with the first — a stadium corner
      needs no agreement at all. Height is fixed, so it cannot
      be anything else. */
border-radius: 999px;

/* FLAT, AND GLASS ONLY IF ASKED. The surface reads --pane,
   the bench's own material token, so it follows the Glass
   dial rather than deciding for itself: 0 resolves to a solid
   board, 100 to the frosted pane. It was a translucent ink
   wash with an inset hairline — glass by every visual measure
   while answering to no control, which is the worst of both,
   because it could not be turned off.

   And it picks up Fill for free: flat resolves --pane to
   --board, and Fill redeclares --board, so a dark fill gives
   a dark pill without this rule naming a colour.

   The edge is the same story. It is a transparent ::before
   until Stroke colours it — a hairline nobody switched on is
   a hairline the control cannot remove. */
background: var(--pane);

/* 4 · ONE NUMBER DRIVES EVERYTHING. The width is sprung in
      JS; the radius, the placeholder's opacity and its slide
      are all read off how far through that spring it is. That
      is the whole reason the transformation reads as
      continuous — with one source there is nothing that can
      arrive at the wrong time relative to anything else. */
const p = (w - SHUT) / (OPEN - SHUT);
--say: clamp((p - 0.55) / 0.45, 0, 1);   /* the last third */

/* THE PRESS IS A REAL BEAT. A click compresses the object for
   90ms before it expands: a thing that yields before it moves
   reads as having been pushed, and a thing that only moves
   reads as having been triggered. Long enough to feel, short
   enough that nobody waits for it. */

/* FOCUS LANDS WITH THE EXPANSION, not at the end of it, so
   the caret is already there when the field arrives. Waiting
   for the width to settle puts a visible pause between the
   box being ready and the box being usable. */

/* THE MAGNET is measured from the FRAME, which never moves,
   and not from the object, which does. A vector read off the
   thing it is displacing is a feedback loop — it converges,
   but it converges by ringing, and on an object this small
   the ring is visible as a shiver.

   A few pixels, and the ceiling is the whole design: past
   about seven it stops being a thing that acknowledges you
   and starts being a thing you are dragging around. */
const pull = (1 - d / R) ** 1.4 * (2 + (give / 100) * 5);

/* And it is off once open. A field that drifts toward the
   pointer while you are trying to click into it is a field
   fighting you. */

params.label: Give
params.hint: how far it leans toward the cursor

params.label: Spring
params.hint: how the width settles

params.label: Width
params.hint: the field at rest

name: Escape button
css:
/* A button that slides away from the cursor, and then stops.

   READ THIS PART FIRST. Near-miss targeting is one hop from a
   genuine dark pattern: the same mechanism aimed the other way
   is a close button that drifts out from under a finger, a
   Decline placed a little harder to hit than an Accept, an
   unsubscribe that needs a second go. It is the same code. It
   is not the same thing only because of the count below.

   What keeps this on the right side of the line:
     · it gives in on its own, after a fixed number of tries
     · it gives in within a few seconds, every time
     · a keyboard never sees it move at all
   Remove any one of those and you have shipped the pattern
   you were imitating. */

/* The vector from the button's HOME to the cursor, in the
   button's own pixels — a board may be drawn at any zoom, and
   a rect comes back in screen ones. Home, not the button's
   current rect: measuring off a box the displacement has just
   moved is a feedback loop, and it converges by RINGING. Ten
   events at one fixed cursor point gave 21, 35, 26, 32, 28,
   30, 29px — a ±6px shiver on a 40px pill, re-seeded by every
   event. The field never moves and the button is centred in
   it, so the field's centre is home. */
const box = field.getBoundingClientRect();
const k   = box.width / field.offsetWidth;
const dx  = (cursor.x - (box.left + box.width / 2)) / k;
const dy  = (cursor.y - (box.top + box.height / 2)) / k;
const distance = Math.hypot(dx, dy);

/* SQUARED, not linear. The button has to be almost inert at
   the edge of its field and bolt over the last third —
   linear made it drift away from a cursor two rooms distant,
   which reads as a bug rather than as nerves. */
const flee  = (1 - distance / radius) ** 2;
const reach = 14 + (skittishness / 100) * 106;

/* The field paints nothing. It was a grey well, on the
   reasoning that an invisible boundary reads as the button
   sticking — right about a SMALL boundary, wrong about the
   component. At 300x160 the clamp sat fifty pixels from home
   and the button hit it constantly, so the wall had to be
   drawn to explain itself; and a drawn wall is a widget in a
   box, which is the one thing here that has a frame round it.
   At 360x240 the clamp is over a hundred pixels out and is
   almost never reached, so it needs no explaining. The box
   still exists — it is what the travel is clamped to and what
   home is measured from — it simply has no surface. */

/* Away, and never out of its own container. The direction is
   undefined when the cursor is exactly on home and INVERTS as
   it crosses — which is the good behaviour rather than a bug:
   the button darts around you to the other side instead of
   being walked into a corner. Held through the undefined
   frame, and the flip travels rather than teleporting. */
if (distance > 6) dir = { x: -dx / distance, y: -dy / distance };
x = clamp(dir.x * flee * reach, -room.x, room.x);
y = clamp(dir.y * flee * reach, -room.y, room.y);

/* ONE DODGE PER APPROACH. Counting every frame inside the
   radius spends the whole joke in a third of a second; the
   flag re-arms only on the way out of the full field, so one
   sweep through is one dodge however fast it was. */
if (distance < radius * 0.55 && armed) { armed = false; dodges++; }
if (distance > radius) armed = true;

/* Two durations behind one attribute. Fleeing is short —
   long enough that the dart across the cursor travels, short
   enough that it is never a wind-up. Coming home is soft,
   because that one is a relief rather than a reaction. */
.esc-btn            { transition: transform 620ms cubic-bezier(.22,1.12,.36,1); }
.esc-btn[data-fled] { transition: transform 130ms cubic-bezier(.3,.8,.4,1); }

/* Reduced motion takes the travel and leaves the joke: the
   count still runs, it still gives in on the same dodge, and
   the button never leaves the middle. */

/* ── Fill and Stroke ─────────────────────────────────────────
   The surface reads the stage's fill tokens with its own value
   left as the var() FALLBACK rather than as a second
   declaration underneath, which is what lets one line serve
   both cases.

   And both happen. .bench-app carries a data-fill of its own
   that follows the theme, so on the wall this is already
   filled and the overlay's control is a choice to DIFFER from
   the bench rather than a switch from nothing. The fallback is
   for a surface mounted outside .bench-app altogether —
   which is what this file is for, since a block lifted out of
   this project has to draw.

   --fill-on-rgb rather than --fill-on wherever the ink is not
   at full strength, because a fallback has to nest inside the
   rgba() to survive: rgba(var(--fill-on-rgb, var(--ink-rgb)), .78).

   The hairline hangs on a ::before that is transparent until
   [data-stroke="on"] colours it — the same ::before every
   other surface on the bench uses. Nothing here is glass, so
   there is no lit rim for the stroke to lose to: the hairline
   is the only edge these can have. */
